title: Sleep Better
subtitle: Wind down well and wake up rested

habit.title: Head to bed on time
habit.description: Get into bed within about 30 minutes of your bedtime
habit.smallerVersion: Get into bed within an hour of your bedtime, or simply keep your wake-up time steady

steps.buttonLabel: Add "Head to bed on time" to my evening
tips: Pick a cue you won't miss, like putting the last dish away or switching off the main light.
Running late? Skip the extras and do just the last steps: teeth, lights, bed.
Not sleepy at bedtime? Get into bed anyway and read a few pages in dim light. You don't have to fall asleep by any deadline.
Heading to bed on time is the goal, not instant sleep. Sleep arrives in its own time.
steps.completionMessage: Your body clock is getting a clearer signal. Next, let's make your sleep space a place that says sleep.
steps.title: Steady Bedtime

letter.title: Your Body Loves a Rhythm
letter.body:
Dear {name},

Think about how your body handles lunch. If you eat at about the same time every day, you start feeling hungry right on schedule. Sleep works in a similar way. Deep in your brain sits a master clock that runs on a roughly 24-hour cycle, and it learns when to make you sleepy and when to make you alert.

When bedtime and wake-up time jump around, that clock gets mixed signals. Studies of students and workers have linked irregular sleep schedules with poorer sleep quality and more daytime tiredness. Many people know the feeling of "social jet lag": sleeping in on days off, then feeling groggy and out of step when the routine restarts.

So our first habit isn't about sleeping more. It's about giving your body a clearer pattern: **head to bed on time, within about 30 minutes of your bedtime.**

Your bedtime is currently set to **{bedTime}** and your wake-up time to **{wakeTime}**. Look at the hours between them. Do they leave enough time for you to feel rested? Many adults do well with seven to nine hours, but needs vary, so trust how you feel. If those times don't match your real life, change them in Settings. A time you can truly keep beats an ambitious one you can't.

**How to make it stick**

- Choose your wake-up time first. It's the easier of the two to keep steady, and bedtime tends to follow.
- On your days off, aim to stay within about an hour of your usual times.
- Not sleepy at bedtime? Get into bed anyway and read a few pages in dim light. Watching the clock rarely helps.
- If shifts, a baby or caring for someone make fixed times impossible, pick the steadiest pattern your life allows. Even one anchor, such as your wake-up time, helps.
- Short naps, a siesta or shifting sleep around fasting or festivals can be fine. Keep naps short and earlier in the day, and anchor your wake-up time as best you can.
- Heading to bed on time is the goal, not instant sleep. Sleep arrives in its own time. If you're awake and frustrated for a good while, Step 7 has a kinder plan than lying there.

**Stack it:** *"After I brush my teeth, I get into bed."*

Your challenge: **be in bed within about 30 minutes of {bedTime} on 3 of the next 5 days.**

Some nights will run late, and that's completely fine. We're building a pattern, not a perfect record.

Here's to steady nights,
Your Fab Life coach

goal.title: Make your sleep space darker, cooler and quieter
goal.description: Choose one or two small changes before your next sleep: block light, keep it comfortably cool, soften noise

steps.buttonLabel: I'll do it before my next sleep
steps.completionMessage: A calm, comfortable space gives sleep an easier path. Next we'll look at the screens that keep us up.
steps.title: A Sleep-Friendly Bedroom

letter.title: Make Your Room Say Sleep
letter.body:
Dear {name},

Have you ever slept wonderfully somewhere dark, cool and still, like a relative's home after the rain or a quiet guest room, and wondered why you can't sleep like that at home? Your surroundings talk to your body all night, even when you're not aware of it.

Research suggests that light, temperature and noise can all affect how well you sleep. Light, even fairly dim, can nudge your body clock and may make sleep lighter for some people. Your body temperature naturally drops as you fall asleep, and a very warm room can get in the way. Sudden sounds can nudge you out of deep sleep even when you don't fully wake.

Today there's no habit to repeat. It's **one small action, done before your next sleep: make your sleep space a little darker, cooler and quieter.** You don't need to do everything, and you don't need to spend anything. Pick the one or two changes that suit your home.

1. **Darker.** Draw the curtains, hang a thicker cloth or sheet over the window, or wear a comfortable eye mask. Turn glowing clocks away or face them to the wall, and put a small piece of tape over tiny standby lights. Never cover a charger, adapter or anything that's plugged in, because they need air to stay cool.
2. **Cooler.** Use a ceiling or table fan, a thin cotton sheet over a heavy blanket and light clothes, or take a cool wash before bed. Open a window earlier in the evening if it's safe and the air is clean. If mosquitoes, smoke, noise or security are a worry, a net, a closed window or a fan alone is fine. Sleep experts often suggest around 18°C (65°F), but in a hot climate the aim is simply as cool as you comfortably can. In cold weather, or if you feel the cold easily, don't chill the room. Keep your usual warmth and aim for comfortable, not cold.
3. **Quieter.** Close doors, add soft furnishings or try earplugs. A steady background hum can also soften sudden noises like traffic, neighbours or a snoring partner. Use the **Try Fan hum** shortcut on this step, then tap **Play**. It's a generated ambient sound, and you can set a sleep timer so it fades out by itself. Keep it quiet, at or below the level of a soft conversation, and play it from the phone's speaker rather than earbuds.

One caution on quiet. If you have a baby or someone who may need you in the night, skip the earplugs, keep the door open or use a baby monitor, and keep the hum low. Everyone should be able to hear the smoke alarm.

Share a room, or sleep in a living space? Small steps still count. An eye mask costs very little, and agreeing a "lights down" time with the people around you can help everyone.

If you often wake up coughing, wheezing or gasping, or someone notices that you stop breathing in the night, please see a doctor rather than relying on tweaks to your space.

Once you've made your changes, come back and tap **Mark as done**.

Sweet dreams,
Your Fab Life coach

habit.title: Screens away before bed
habit.description: Put phones, TV and tablets away 30 to 60 minutes before bed
habit.smallerVersion: Put your phone down 10 minutes before bed

tips: Charge your phone out of reach of your pillow, if that's safe for you, except when you start a Fab Life wind-down.
Put a book or a radio where your phone used to sit, so your hand finds something else.
On call, caring for someone, or using your phone for medical alerts? Keep it within hearing and let only those alerts and key contacts through.
Short on time? Just 10 minutes without screens is your smaller version.
steps.completionMessage: Your mind gets a calmer runway into the night. Next, a look at the afternoon cup that can follow you to bed.
steps.title: Screens Away

letter.title: Let the Screens Say Goodnight
letter.body:
Dear {name},

"Just one more episode." "I'll check one message." Twenty minutes later you're deep in a comment thread, wide awake, wondering where the evening went. Screens are designed to hold our attention, and getting pulled in isn't a personal failing. It's clever design doing its job.

Two things seem to be going on. First, bright light from phones, tablets and TVs, especially in a dark room and close to your face, can delay the release of melatonin, a hormone that helps signal night-time to your body. How strongly it affects you depends on brightness, distance and how long you look. Second, the content itself keeps your mind busy: news, messages, work emails and videos are stimulating. Researchers are still working out how much comes from the light and how much from the engagement, but putting screens away helps with both.

Your new habit: **put screens away 30 to 60 minutes before bed.** Start with 30. If that sounds like a lot, the smaller version is just 10 minutes. "Screens away" means no scrolling, TV, email or games. Later in this journey, Fab Life's own stretch and wind-down will be the exception: you'll open one on low brightness, start it, then set the phone down.

**Making it practical**

- Charge your phone out of reach of your pillow, if that's safe for you. Out of reach is easier than out of sight.
- Need an alarm? A cheap alarm clock does the job, or leave your phone face-down out of arm's reach.
- Fill the gap with something gentle: a paper book, a radio programme, soft music, a chat with family, a slow walk around the house or a light tidy-up. Audio is fine as long as the screen stays dark. Fab Life's sounds keep playing with the screen off, so you can start one and put the phone down.
- On call, caring for someone, living alone, or using your phone for medical alerts (such as a glucose monitor) or as your only way to call for help? Keep it within hearing, and set Do Not Disturb to let those alerts and key contacts through while it silences the rest. Safety comes before this habit.
- Dimming the brightness or using night mode can help a little, but they don't replace putting the screen away.

If late-night scrolling is how you cope with worry or loneliness, you're far from alone. Talking with someone you trust, or a counsellor or doctor, can help with whatever sits underneath.

**Stack it:** *"After I finish my last task of the evening, I plug my phone in away from my pillow."*

Your challenge: **put screens away for 30 minutes before bed on 3 of the next 5 days.**

Good night for now,
Your Fab Life coach

habit.title: Caffeine cut-off
habit.description: Have your last caffeinated drink about 8 hours before bed (for many people, early to mid afternoon)
habit.smallerVersion: Swap just your last caffeinated drink of the day for water, herbal tea or decaf

tips: Bedtime 10:30 PM? Last cup by 2:30 PM. Don't drink caffeine at all? Lovely, just tick this one off.
Cut down gradually if you drink a lot. Swap one cup at a time.
Keep a caffeine-free favourite ready: warm water, herbal tea, decaf, warm milk, a plant-based drink or buttermilk, whatever suits you.
Check labels. Cola, energy drinks, some teas, chocolate and some headache tablets contain caffeine.
steps.completionMessage: Your afternoons are now kinder to your nights. Next, a gentle stretch to ease your body at the end of the day.
steps.gentleNote: Sensitive stomach? Warm water, a mild herbal tea such as fennel (saunf), or a ripe banana, plain toast or curd are gentle choices. Strong tea or coffee on an empty stomach can bother some people, so have something small first.
steps.title: Caffeine Cut-Off

letter.title: The Cup That Follows You to Bed
letter.body:
Dear {name},

It's 4 p.m. The post-lunch slump arrives, and a hot cup of chai or coffee, or a cold can, looks like the perfect rescue. It often is, for a while. But the cup that carries you through the afternoon may still be quietly at work at bedtime.

Caffeine works partly by blocking adenosine, a natural chemical that builds up during the day and makes you feel sleepy. On average it takes around five hours for your body to clear half the caffeine from a drink, though this varies a lot from person to person. Pregnancy, some medicines and your genes can all slow it down. In one small study using a fairly large dose, about the caffeine in several cups of coffee, caffeine taken six hours before bed still cut sleep time, even though people didn't always notice. A smaller afternoon cup may affect you less, and people differ a lot.

Your new habit is the only afternoon one in this journey: **a caffeine cut-off.** Have your last coffee, strong tea, cola or energy drink about 8 hours before bed. Count back 8 hours from {bedTime} and that's your cut-off. For a bedtime of 10:30 PM, that's 2:30 PM, and for many people it lands somewhere in the early to mid afternoon. Keep your morning cup if you love it. This is about moving the last one earlier, not giving it up. If your Afternoon reminder arrives later than your cut-off, change its time in Settings under Rituals & reminders.

**Tips**

- Cut down gradually if you drink a lot. Stopping suddenly can bring headaches and tiredness for a few days.
- Keep a favourite caffeine-free option ready: warm water, herbal tea, decaf, warm milk, a plant-based drink, buttermilk or fruit-infused water. Decaf is optional, and so is anything that doesn't suit your stomach.
- Beat the slump another way: a glass of water, five minutes outdoors in daylight, a short walk or desk stretch, or a small snack like curd, a banana, plain toast or a few nuts if they suit you.
- Check labels. Cola, energy drinks, some teas, chocolate and some headache tablets contain caffeine too.
- Work nights? Count back from your sleep time, but never at the cost of staying alert while driving, using machinery or caring for others. Cut back gradually, keep your caffeine earlier in the shift where you can, and ask your doctor or occupational health service about a plan that is safe for you.

If you're pregnant, have a heart rhythm problem, high blood pressure or anxiety, or take regular medicines, ask your doctor how much caffeine is right for you, and check herbal teas with them too. If caffeine makes you jittery or gives you palpitations, cut back and mention it to a doctor.

**Stack it:** *"After I finish my last caffeinated cup of the day, I fill a glass of water."*

Your challenge: **keep your caffeine cut-off on 4 of the next 6 days.**

Cheers to calmer evenings,
Your Fab Life coach

habit.title: Gentle evening stretch
habit.description: 5 to 10 minutes of slow stretching to ease the day out of your body
habit.smallerVersion: Stretch for one minute: reach up, roll your shoulders and breathe out slowly

tips: Move slowly and stop at a mild pull. Stretching should never hurt.
On the floor, in bed or in a chair all work. Choose what feels comfortable.
Leave a little time after dinner, and skip lying-down moves if they bring on heartburn.
Tap Start on the habit for the Evening Stretch, a slow floor sequence with a timer. Skip any move that doesn't feel right, or use the chair ideas in your letter.
steps.completionMessage: Your body now has a gentle way to put the day down. Next, a way to quiet the thoughts.
steps.title: Gentle Evening Stretch

letter.title: Let Your Body Unclench
letter.body:
Dear {name},

By evening, many of us are carrying the day in our bodies: shoulders creeping towards our ears, a stiff neck from the desk, tight hips from sitting, tired legs from standing. A body that feels tense can be hard to settle at night.

Research suggests that people who are regularly active tend to sleep better, and some small studies of gentle practices like stretching and yoga have found modest improvements in sleep quality. The evidence isn't perfect, but for most people the risk is low and many people find it helps. A few slow minutes also work as a signal: they tell your body, and your mind, that the day is winding down.

This week's small step: **a gentle evening stretch of 5 to 10 minutes.** Keep it slow and easy. This isn't a workout, and you shouldn't feel out of breath.

**How to do it your way**

- Tap **Start** on the habit to open the Evening Stretch routine, if it's offered for your settings. It's a slow sequence of about 10 minutes with a built-in timer and, for some moves, an easier version. Most of it is done on the floor, so a mat or blanket helps. Skip or soften any move that doesn't feel right, such as Child's pose or Legs up the wall, and stop whenever you like. Five minutes counts.
- Prefer to sit, or find the floor hard? Try your own mini-routine in a chair: slow neck turns, shoulder rolls, a gentle seated twist, side bends and a few long breaths out. If you move from a chair, Explore → Move has seated stretches too, such as Desk Reset.
- In bed? Hug your knees gently towards your chest, let your knees drop to one side for a slow lying twist, and circle your ankles and wrists.
- Move into a mild pull, never into pain. Hold each stretch for about 20 to 30 seconds and breathe out as you ease a little further.
- Lower the lights and your screen brightness, and let your breathing slow down. Leave a little time after dinner, and skip lying-down moves if they bring on heartburn.

If you have an injury, back or joint problems, are pregnant, or often feel dizzy, check with a doctor or physiotherapist about which stretches are right for you. Skip anything that doesn't feel good.

**Stack it:** *"After my screens are away, I stretch for five minutes, with my phone propped nearby on low brightness if I want the timer."*

Your challenge: **stretch gently for 5 minutes on 3 of the next 5 days.**

On a tired night, one minute of reaching up and breathing out still counts.

Slow and easy,
Your Fab Life coach

habit.title: Evening brain dump
habit.description: Write down what's on your mind, plus one thing that went well today
habit.smallerVersion: Write just one line: one thing that went okay today, or one thing for tomorrow

steps.buttonLabel: Add "Evening brain dump" to my evening
tips: Two minutes is plenty. Set a timer if it helps.
Write tomorrow's to-dos as a short list, then close the notebook.
The Fab Life journal is on your phone, so write before your screens-away time, or use paper later.
No grammar needed, any language, any style. Typing hard? Use voice typing, or say it out loud.
steps.completionMessage: You now have a place to put your thoughts down for the night. Next, a guided way to wind down.
steps.title: Evening Brain Dump

letter.title: Empty Your Mind onto the Page
letter.body:
Dear {name},

It's the middle of dinner and you're nodding along to the conversation when a thought lands: *did I ever answer that email?* You can't do anything about it right now, so it goes onto a mental sticky note. Hours later, in the quiet, that sticky note is still tapping you on the shoulder. Unfinished business has a way of waiting for the dark.

Researchers who study sleep find that a busy, worried mind is one of the most common reasons people struggle to drop off. In one small sleep-lab study at Baylor University, young adults who spent five minutes writing a to-do list before bed tended to fall asleep faster than people who wrote about what they had already done. That study looked at to-do lists, so if worries are circling, a short list of tomorrow's tasks is the best-supported option. Other research suggests that noting what you're grateful for may help some people feel calmer and sleep a little better. These are small studies and results vary, but the idea makes sense: a page can hold what your head keeps trying to hold.

Here's the habit: **an evening brain dump.** Spend two minutes writing whatever is on your mind, then add one thing that went well today.

**How to do it**

- Tap **Write** on the habit to open the journal. The Reflection page has a free text box, so you can write whatever you like, even if the prompt asks something else. For something quicker, open the Gratitude page in Explore → Mind → Journal and write three short lines.
- Any format works: a list for tomorrow, a few sentences about a worry, or one honest line like "Today was hard, and I got through it."
- You don't need to solve anything. For a worry you can't act on tonight, write "Not tonight. I'll look at this tomorrow," and let it rest.
- Your phone is a screen, so do this before your screens-away time, or use a paper notebook beside the bed. Entries in Fab Life stay on your phone and you can delete them any time. In Settings → My habits you can move this habit to the top of your evening.
- Write in any language. Nobody is marking it. Typing hard? Use your keyboard's voice typing, or just say it out loud and list tomorrow's three things.

If you often feel low or hopeless, or worries feel heavy or constant, please talk to a doctor, a counsellor or someone you trust. If you ever have thoughts of harming yourself, please contact your local emergency number or a crisis helpline right away. You don't have to face the night alone. A notebook can help, but it isn't a substitute for support. And if writing about worries leaves you more wound up, switch to a short to-do list or the gratitude lines, do it earlier in the evening, or skip it.

**Stack it:** *"After dinner is cleared away, I take two minutes to write."*

Your challenge: **do your evening brain dump on 3 of the next 5 days.**

Gently,
Your Fab Life coach

habit.title: Sleep wind-down
habit.description: A 10-minute guided wind-down in bed or a comfortable chair
habit.smallerVersion: Listen for just a few minutes, or take five slow breaths with a long breath out

tips: Get comfortable first, then tap Listen, dim the screen and set your phone face-down within reach.
Still awake afterwards? Resting quietly is gentler on you than fighting to sleep.
Racing mind? Try Unload your worries, a 6-minute session in Explore → Mind.
Sharing a room? Keep the volume low or use earphones for the session, and the captions carry it if you can't hear well.
steps.completionMessage: Your evening now has a calm ending. One last step brings it all together.
steps.title: Sleep Wind-Down

letter.title: Teach Your Mind to Land
letter.body:
Dear {name},

Think of a child's bedtime: a warm bath, a story, a song, the lights going down one by one. Somewhere along the way, most of us stopped giving ourselves that gentle runway into sleep, then expect it to arrive on command. It isn't a failure of willpower. A busy day usually needs a way down.

Here's the helpful paradox: the harder we try to fall asleep, the more alert we tend to become. So instead of trying, we practise letting go and giving attention somewhere gentle to rest. Research suggests that relaxation practices such as slow breathing, body scans and mindfulness may help some people feel calmer at bedtime, though the effects are modest and differ from person to person.

Your new habit: **a sleep wind-down.** In bed or a comfortable chair, tap **Listen** on the habit to hear the 10-minute Sleep wind-down, a calm guided session read aloud by your phone's voice, with captions on screen. Start it, turn the brightness down and set the phone face-down within reach. You can close your eyes and just listen. Sharing a room? Keep the volume low or use earphones for the session, take them out before you sleep, and let the captions carry it if you can't hear well.

**For a racing mind, you have more tools in Explore → Mind**

- **Listen** to *Unload your worries* (6 minutes), a guided session for when thoughts keep circling.
- **Breathe** with *4-7-8 breathing*. Beginners can start with just three rounds. If the holds feel uncomfortable, just breathe normally during them, or choose *Long exhale*, which has no hold.
- **Play** a quiet sound such as Rain, Ocean waves, Fan hum or Brown noise. They're generated sounds, not recordings. Keep the volume low, use the phone's speaker rather than earbuds, and let the sleep timer fade them out.

And when you're lying awake anyway? That's normal, and nothing to fear. Resting quietly is gentler on you than fighting to sleep, and it may still help your body unwind, so try not to check the clock. If you feel wide awake and frustrated after a good while, many people find it helps to get up, sit somewhere dim, read a few quiet pages, and return to bed when sleepy. Only get up if that feels safe: keep the light low but enough to see where you're stepping, and take your time. If getting up is hard, or you share the room, sit up in bed with a small dim lamp or book light, or rest in a bedside chair, and lie back down when sleepy.

If you have asthma, a lung or heart condition, or you feel light-headed when you breathe slowly or hold your breath, check with your doctor before trying breathing exercises. Stop and breathe normally if you feel dizzy, tingly or anxious. If you're pregnant or prone to panic, ask your doctor first, or stick with Long exhale.

**Stack it:** *"After I get into bed, I tap Listen, dim the screen and set my phone face-down."*

Your challenge: **do a sleep wind-down on 3 of the next 5 days.**

Rest easy,
Your Fab Life coach

tips: Tap Start ritual each evening and let the app take you through your habits one at a time.
On tired nights, do the smaller version of every habit.
Judge your sleep over a few weeks, not by a single night.
steps.completionMessage: Your evening ritual is complete. Read your final letter.
steps.title: Your Evening Ritual

letter.title: Putting Your Evening Together
letter.body:
Dear {name},

This is the final step of your Sleep Better journey. Look at what you've put together for your evenings:

1. **A brain dump**, to empty your head onto the page
2. **Screens away**, to let your mind slow down
3. **A gentle stretch**, to ease your body
4. **Heading to bed on time**, so your body clock knows the plan
5. **A sleep wind-down**, in bed, to help your mind land

Your afternoon caffeine cut-off keeps working in the background. It isn't part of this challenge, but it's part of the picture, and your sleep space is already set up for rest.

Your challenge: **complete your whole evening ritual on 5 of the next 7 days.**

Habits take time to become automatic. Research from University College London found that it took people anywhere from a few weeks to many months, typically around two months. You've been building this for weeks already.

**A few things to remember**

- **Use the ritual player.** Tap **Start ritual** and the app walks you through your evening habits, one at a time. When a step uses your phone, keep the brightness low, then set it down.
- **Check the order.** The app lists habits in the order you added them, so "Head to bed on time" may sit at the top. Open Settings → My habits (or the Today menu → Edit my habits) and use the arrows to put them in the order above, so the evening flows the way your night does.
- **Time and tired nights.** A full evening takes about 25 minutes. On a tired night, do the smaller version of each habit: one line, 10 minutes without screens, a one-minute stretch, a few breaths, in bed. That's about 5 minutes, and a tiny ritual still counts. Rotating shifts? Update your bedtime in Settings when your shift changes, and set your day start under Your day if you go to bed after 3 AM.
- **Don't grade single nights.** Sleep naturally shifts with stress, heat, illness and busy days. Look at the trend over a few weeks instead: how do you feel in the morning, and how is your energy?
- **Optional numbers.** If you like data, Fab Life can show last night's sleep from Health Connect, but only if you choose to connect it. Sleep estimates from phones and other apps are rough, so how you feel matters more. If tracking makes you anxious about sleep, skip it entirely.

If, after weeks of steady habits, you still sleep poorly, that isn't failing the journey. A doctor can help, and asking is one way of looking after yourself.

Five evenings out of seven. You can do this.

Sleep well,
Your Fab Life coach

introLetter.title: Better Nights Start in the Evening
introLetter.body:
Dear {name},

It's 2 a.m. You check the clock, work out how many hours are left, and your mind helpfully starts listing everything you forgot to do. If that sounds familiar, you're in very good company. Almost everyone has nights like this.

Here's the gentle truth about sleep: you can't force it. Trying harder to fall asleep usually backfires. What you *can* do is set up the conditions in which sleep tends to arrive on its own. Research suggests that a steady rhythm, a calm bedroom, less late-night stimulation and a quiet wind-down help many people sleep more easily. Those are habits, and habits can be learned.

Over the next few weeks we'll build a calm **evening ritual**, one small habit at a time, plus a single afternoon habit and a one-time sleep-space reset. You'll practise each step for a few days before we add the next.

A few things worth knowing before we begin:

- **Sleep needs vary.** Many adults feel best with around seven to nine hours, but some need a little less or more, and sleep often changes with age. The goal is to feel rested, not to match anyone else's number.
- **Consistency matters more than perfection.** A good rhythm most nights beats a flawless week followed by a collapse.
- **Lying awake is common.** Being awake and worrying in the night is not a failure, and it doesn't mean you're doing this wrong. We'll look at kind ways to handle it.
- **Real life counts.** If a baby, a night shift, caring for someone, a siesta or fasting changes your nights, we'll look for whatever fits your life.

One important note. This journey is a friendly coach, not a treatment for insomnia or any other sleep condition. It uses everyday habits only, with no pills or supplements. If you already take medicine for sleep, please don't change it without asking your doctor.

Please talk to a doctor if your sleep trouble has lasted for weeks, if you often feel low, if you snore loudly or you (or someone who sleeps near you) notice that you stop breathing at night, or if you feel very sleepy during the day. If you do feel very sleepy, please don't drive or use machinery until you're alert. A doctor can look into what's going on and point you to the right help, and these habits can sit alongside that care.

Your first step is about rhythm, and you can make it as gentle as you need. Let's begin.

Sleep well,
Your Fab Life coach

outroLetter.title: Rested, One Evening at a Time
outroLetter.body:
Dear {name},

Take a moment to notice what you've done: **you completed your Sleep Better journey.**

A few weeks ago you started with one simple idea, a steady time for bed. Since then you've shaped a sleep space that invites rest, put your screens down, moved your last coffee earlier, stretched your body, emptied your mind onto a page and learned to land with a guided wind-down. That's a real evening ritual, built one small habit at a time.

The most important lesson isn't about any single habit. It's this: **you can't force sleep, but you can make room for it.** Everything you've practised does exactly that.

**What happens now?**

Keep the parts that help most. You don't have to do all of it every night. On a late evening, a one-minute stretch or five slow breaths still tells your body what comes next. Rough nights will visit again sometimes: stress, travel, illness, hot weather, a baby, a big day. They're normal, they don't undo your progress, and your ritual will be waiting whenever you want it.

If you find yourself lying awake worrying, remember what you've learned. It's common, it's not a failure, and quiet rest is gentler than fighting for sleep. Try *Unload your worries*, *4-7-8 breathing* or a gentle sound, and be kind to yourself.

And please keep an eye on the bigger picture. If sleep trouble lasts for weeks, if you often feel low, if you snore loudly or stop breathing at night, or if you feel very sleepy in the day, talk to a doctor. Until you feel alert, please don't drive or use machinery. Asking for help is one of the wisest habits of all.

When you're ready, more journeys are waiting in your Journeys list, and a rested you is a great place to start any of them.

For tonight, though, simply enjoy getting into bed. You've earned it.

So proud of you,
Your Fab Life coach

missedDaysLetter.title: Missed a Few Days?
missedDaysLetter.body:
Dear {name},

It's been a few evenings since we last spoke, and I want you to know straight away that **that's completely okay.** Nobody has a perfect run of nights.

Evenings, and sometimes afternoons, are the busiest, most unpredictable part of many days. Late meetings, family, festivals, travel, a poorly child or a rough night can all knock a routine off course. Missing a few evenings doesn't undo what you've built, and habits are usually easy to pick back up. What counts is coming back, not never slipping.

Here are a few gentle ways forward:

- **Keep going.** Nothing needs to change. Tonight is a fresh start.
- **Make it smaller.** Every habit has a smaller version: ten minutes without screens, a one-minute stretch, one line in your journal. A small habit you actually do beats a big one you skip.
- **Pick just one.** Choose the easiest evening habit and do only that tonight.

And if poor sleep itself has been getting in the way, you deserve support, from the people around you or from a doctor. These habits will still be here.

No rush at all,
Your Fab Life coach

welcomeBackLetter.title: Welcome Back
welcomeBackLetter.body:
Dear {name},

Welcome back. I'm really glad you're here.

Whatever pulled you away, whether it was a busy stretch, a hard time or a run of late nights, there's no need to explain and nothing to feel guilty about. Opening the app again shows you still care about resting well, and that's what matters.

Here's what hasn't changed: **everything you've built is still here.** The steps you completed and the habits you learned are waiting for you, and your evenings are easier to restart than they feel.

We'll restart your current step from the beginning, so there's no pressure to catch up. For tonight, try just the smaller version of your current step. If you're not sure where to begin, take five slow breaths with a long breath out once you're in bed. That's plenty for a first evening back.

Beginning again is part of every habit.

See you this evening,
Your Fab Life coach
